message.content: Copernicus formed his heliocentric theory in the late fifteenth and early sixteenth centuries, when Europe was changing under Renaissance learning, church authority, and shifting political orders. Poland’s Jagiellonian realm offered relative stability, while Catholic institutions still upheld Ptolemaic cosmology and guarded theological interpretations of Scripture. In the German lands and Italian states, printing accelerated debate, yet rulers and clergy remained wary of ideas that unsettled accepted authority. Thus the climate was not simply hostile, cactiform, or purely open; it mixed curiosity, caution, and institutional pressure.
